Week 1 built the LAE system and simple viability tools (VOT, generalized cost, unit cost, sandboxes). This week asks **who competes with whom**, why **scarce landing space and route density** matter, and when rivals might **share infrastructure** instead of duplicating it.

**Orient refreshers:**

- [How does LAE work?](business-overview.qmd) — roles in the value chain  
- [Companies & sectors](landscape.qmd) — named organisations (not market-share claims)  
- [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd) — institutions and standing caveats  

## Summary {#summary}

**Before you go**

- How market structure shapes competition across different LAE service segments.
- Tools for concentration and market power (including a simple HHI-style check).
- Why utilization, route density, and fixed costs change average cost—and what that means for entry.
- Price competition, capacity limits, entry barriers, and when rivals might cooperate on shared facilities.

**Takeaways**

- Market power in LAE is often tied to scarce infrastructure (e.g. vertiports) and route density.
- Large sunk costs and entry barriers can support limit pricing that keeps rivals out.
- Capacity constraints and differentiation can soften price wars—but they do not guarantee high prices or profits.
- Co-opetition can cut duplicated infrastructure cost if access, investment, and control rules are clear.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Classroom numbers vs absolute facts.** Worked examples below use round figures (shares, rents, flights, fares). They are **illustrative assumptions for learning**, not current Hong Kong market data, corridor forecasts, or named operators’ real costs. Absolute programme facts (first Sandbox **38 of 72**, Sandbox X module counts, corridor caveats) stay with issuers on [Key figures](key-figures.qmd) / [Official status](tracker.qmd) / [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats).
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of Week 2 you should be able to:

1. **Explain** how market structure shapes competition in different LAE services (and why LAE is not one single market).  
2. **Explain** how utilization and route density can reduce average cost when fixed costs are large.  
3. **Identify** main barriers that make entry costly or difficult (including NASA-style categories used in class).  
4. **Use** simple tools — HHI as a screen, average-cost / density equations, limit pricing, Bertrand intuition with capacity, and a co-opetition cost split — to organise an argument.  
5. **Evaluate** how Hong Kong and the wider GBA may contribute complementary capabilities without treating trial participation as proof of market dominance.

## 1. Why market structure matters in LAE

Week 1 asked whether a service might create value and cover cost. Week 2 asks a different managerial question: **in this corridor or segment, who has bargaining power — and why?**

Imagine two operators in Hong Kong airspace. One pushes low prices on drone cargo to the New Territories; another locks scarce air-taxi access toward the airport. They are not only fighting for customers. In a dense city they also fight for **physical landing and handling space** — rooftops, pads, charging, and related access that cannot be duplicated cheaply.

That fight does not look the same in every LAE application. Competition may differ by **service type**, **corridor**, and **infrastructure layer** (aircraft vs sites vs digital coordination vs supporting services). Roles and firm lists for Hong Kong / GBA sit on [How does LAE work?](business-overview.qmd) and [Companies & sectors](landscape.qmd); this week supplies the economic language to interpret them.

### Link back to Week 1

Week 1’s empty-seat / utilization arithmetic already hinted that **fixed site cost ÷ flights** can dominate unit cost. Week 2 explains why that arithmetic becomes a **competitive** weapon: whoever controls scarce pads and dense routes may sustain a lower average cost — and may try to keep rivals from matching that density.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Sandbox note.** Participation in a Hong Kong trial programme (the early **Regulatory Sandbox** or later **Sandbox X**) is evidence about *testing under controlled conditions*. It does **not** by itself establish market dominance or commercial scale. Keep the two programmes separate: first-batch **38 of 72** vs Sandbox X module counts on [Key figures](key-figures.qmd); standing caveats on [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats).
:::

## 2. What economists mean by “market structure”

Before analysing flying taxis or drone corridors, label how competition is organised in a **defined market** (product + geography + customer type — for example “premium passenger trips on a named corridor,” not “all of LAE”).

Three classic structures (simplified):

| Structure | Plain meaning | Everyday analogy (not an LAE claim) |
|-----------|---------------|-------------------------------------|
| **Monopoly** | One provider serves the defined market. Pricing power is still limited by demand, regulation, and substitutes. | A single toll tunnel on a route |
| **Oligopoly** | A small number of large players watch each other; one price cut can trigger responses. | A handful of mobile networks |
| **Perfect competition** | Many small sellers of a homogeneous product; no one can raise price alone. | Many stalls selling the same simple item |

**Core lesson for LAE:** there is no single market structure for the whole low-altitude economy. Last-mile logistics, passenger air taxis, industrial inspection, and emergency medical missions can look like different competitive games — even in the same city.

### Who might compete?

Depending on the market you define, rivals may include aircraft developers and manufacturers; transport and logistics operators; telecommunications and digital-platform providers; infrastructure providers (landing, charging, maintenance); and supporting-service providers (finance, leasing, insurance, certification, professional services). Always state **which layer** you are analysing before talking about “the LAE market.”

**Beyond the slide.** An OEM, a vertiport landlord, and a logistics operator can all be “competitors” only if you fuzz the market definition. Define the **product** (e.g. last-mile B2B parcels under 5 kg on a named corridor) and the **layer** (operator vs site owner). Otherwise HHI and “dominance” become meaningless.

---

## 3. Four segments — four competitive logics

Class organises early LAE battles into four families (aligned with Week 1’s value families, but now with a competition lens):

1. **Last-mile logistics** — speed and cost rule; drones win when they beat road congestion on predictable B2B routes.  
2. **Passenger air taxis** — time is the product; premium travellers may pay for minutes saved on congested corridors.  
3. **Industrial inspection and surveying** — reliability and disruption avoidance matter; buyers pay to inspect assets without shutting ground traffic.  
4. **Emergency medical services (EMS)** — very high willingness to pay when time and access are mission-critical.

Dated trial and operating examples (not market-share claims): [Use cases](usecases.qmd).

### Competitive logic by segment (textbook table)

| Segment | Likely rivalry style | Scarce asset often binding | Softens / intensifies price pressure |
|---------|----------------------|----------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Last-mile logistics | Many routes; cost and reliability | Pads, BVLOS permission, weather windows | Homogeneous parcels → more Bertrand-like if capacity loose |
| Passenger air taxis | Few corridors; brand and schedule | Vertiport slots, noise windows | Differentiation + pad caps can soften wars |
| Inspection | Project / contract markets | Certified capability, data/privacy | Less pure price war; quality and safety cases matter |
| EMS / public | Often procurement / priority rules | Availability, response time | Willingness to pay high; access may be allocated, not auctioned |

**Managerial implication:** do not import a “passenger oligopoly” story into an inspection tender, or a “logistics price war” story into an EMS availability contract (Week 6 payment design).

---

## 4. Market concentration and the HHI screen

**Concentration** asks how much of a defined market’s activity sits with the largest players. If one operator uniquely controls a corridor’s usable landing access, pricing pressure from rivals is weak. If several operators can use the same scarce site under clear rules, prices are more contested.

### Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI)

A common screening measure is:

$$
HHI = \sum_{i=1}^{N} s_i^2
$$

where $s_i$ is firm $i$’s market share **in percent** in the defined market (so a pure monopoly scores $100^2 = 10{,}000$). Squaring **amplifies** large shares: a firm with 90% contributes $8{,}100$; four equal 25% firms contribute $4 \times 625 = 2{,}500$.

Course glossary entry: [HHI](glossary.qmd) (course term).

**Policy use in this course:** HHI is a **screen**. A high score may justify closer look at entry conditions and conduct. It does **not** by itself prove illegal market power or dictate a regulatory response.

### Worked illustration (classroom shares)

**Scenario (illustrative):** shares on a hypothetical delivery corridor under review.

| | Case A: four equal operators | Case B: one large, one small |
|--|------------------------------|------------------------------|
| Shares | 25%, 25%, 25%, 25% | 80%, 20% |
| HHI | $4 \times 25^2 = \mathbf{2{,}500}$ | $80^2 + 20^2 = 6{,}400 + 400 = \mathbf{6{,}800}$ |

Case B is far more concentrated and may warrant closer examination of **entry** and **access to sites** — still without claiming that any real Hong Kong corridor has these shares. (Slide titles that say “Sandbox Dominance” are teaching labels for Case B’s *story* — they do **not** mean Sandbox selection equals market share.)

### Beyond the slide: what HHI does *not* tell you

- It does not identify whether the “pie” is seats, flights, revenue, or pad movements — you must define the metric.  
- It does not prove that high concentration came from exclusionary conduct rather than superior density or early site leases.  
- It ignores **substitutes** outside the defined market (road delivery, Airport Express, manned inspection). Week 1’s generalized-cost logic still bounds pricing power.

## 5. Fixed cost, marginal cost, and average cost per flight

To see why landing pads and utilization dominate LAE competition, separate two cost ideas:

- **Fixed costs** — paid even if you fly zero customers (for example a long lease on a rooftop site).  
- **Marginal (variable) cost** — the extra cost of one more flight (energy, minor wear, and similar).

Average total cost per flight (simple teaching form):

$$
\text{ATC} = \frac{\text{Fixed costs}}{\text{Number of flights}} + \text{Marginal cost}
$$

More flights **spread** the fixed charge. Low utilization makes each flight look extremely expensive even if energy is cheap.

### Worked illustration (rooftop rent)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** rooftop pad lease **HK$1,000,000 per month** ≈ **HK$33,333 per day**; marginal cost **HK$50 per flight**.

| | Low utilization (20 flights/day) | High utilization (200 flights/day) |
|--|----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Fixed cost per flight | $33{,}333 / 20 =$ **HK$1,667** | $33{,}333 / 200 =$ **HK$167** |
| + Marginal cost | HK$50 | HK$50 |
| **ATC** | **HK$1,717** | **HK$217** |

**Takeaway:** high fixed site costs make low utilization deadly. Operators must earn enough reliable daily volume — subject to demand, weather, regulation, and pad throughput (Week 5 deepens infrastructure).

### Connection to Week 1 and to HHI

Week 1’s operating-restriction example (same fixed lease, fewer flights) is the same ATC logic under a **noise window** shock. Week 2 adds the competitive twist: if only one firm can reach 200 flights/day because it alone has pad access, ATC gaps can **look like** a moat — and HHI may later rise on that corridor. Causation runs from **scarce sites → density → ATC → possible concentration**, not from “HHI causes low cost.”

---

## 6. Economies of density (not bigger vehicles)

Traditional airlines often chase **economies of scale** with larger aircraft. Many LAE concepts cannot “go bigger” the same way: passenger eVTOL ideas may have only a handful of seats; delivery drones carry limited payload. Hong Kong has **no dedicated eVTOL statute yet**; treat eVTOL as an industry concept pending rules ([Week 1](week-01.qmd); [Glossary · vehicles](glossary.qmd#vehicles-and-operations)).

Instead, LAE economics leans on **economies of density**: running **more volume through the same corridor and sites** so fixed route and pad costs are spread thinly. Achievable density is limited by demand, pad capacity, congestion, weather, and rules — density is not a free lunch ([Glossary · economies of density](glossary.qmd)).

A teaching form that highlights density in the denominator:

$$
\text{Average cost per flight} = \frac{\text{Fixed route costs}}{\text{Flights} \times \text{Density factor}} + \text{Marginal cost}
$$

(In the simplest classroom cases, “density” is just higher flight count on the same fixed pad.)

**Incumbent angle:** an operator that already has volume and site access may sustain a lower average cost than a thin entrant — one reason early control of scarce pads can look like a competitive moat. **Network effects** (a wider network is more useful to customers) are related but conceptually distinct from density on one corridor (Week 8 / Week 12 return to networks).

### Worked illustration (density trap)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** fixed pad cost **HK$50,000/day**; marginal cost **HK$100/flight**.

| | Operator A: 20 flights/day | Operator B: 500 flights/day |
|--|----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Fixed per flight | HK$2,500 | HK$100 |
| + MC | HK$100 | HK$100 |
| **Cost per flight** | **HK$2,600** | **HK$200** |

Under these assumptions B has a much lower average cost. Whether 500 flights/day is operationally or commercially feasible is a separate evidence question — Week 5 throughput and Week 8 congestion tools test that claim.

**Beyond the slide.** Do not treat “500 flights/day” as a Hong Kong forecast. Use it only to see how steeply ATC falls with density *if* demand and pad rules allow it.

---

## 7. Entry barriers: a NASA-style checklist

NASA’s UAM market work (2018) is used in this course as a **practical checklist** of why new entrants struggle — not as Hong Kong law. Three barriers emphasised in class:

1. **Regulatory / certification** — years of testing, documentation, and approvals before routine paying operations (the “valley of death” for capital).  
2. **Infrastructure availability** — scarce sites, power, and related ground systems in a land-constrained city.  
3. **Public perception** — noise, privacy, or visual concerns that can shrink operating windows or close corridors.

Importance varies by application and over time. Hong Kong’s institutional map (Working Group, TLB, CAD, OFCA) is on [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd); citeable programme status is on [Official status](tracker.qmd). Cap. **448G** risk-based SUA regulation and advanced-ops permissions (Week 7) are the local legal frame for light unmanned craft — distinct from US “Part 25”-style manned-aviation stories used only as comparators in Week 1.

### Sunk costs

A **sunk cost** is expenditure you cannot recover if you exit (for example much of the spend on a one-off approval process that cannot be resold). High sunk entry costs deter startups; incumbents may benefit because rivals must “pay to show up” before competing on price.

**Contrast with recoverable assets.** A van you can resell is not fully sunk. A corridor-specific safety case or a pad build-out with no alternative tenant may be largely sunk.

### Limit pricing

If an incumbent could charge a very high monopoly price, that profit signal might attract entry. **Limit pricing** means charging low enough that a potential entrant’s expected average cost (including amortised sunk entry cost) is not covered — a teaching strategy, not a guarantee that entry is blocked.

$$
P_{\text{Limit}} \approx AC_{\text{Entrant}} = \frac{\text{Sunk entry cost}}{\text{Expected volume } Q} + MC
$$

### Worked illustration (limit price and shared pads)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** entrant expects $Q = 10{,}000$ flights; $MC =$ HK$200.

| | High sunk entry (own pad build-out) | Lower sunk entry (shared pad access) |
|--|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Sunk entry cost | HK$10,000,000 | HK$1,000,000 |
| $AC_{\text{Entrant}}$ | $1{,}000 + 200 =$ **HK$1,200** | $100 + 200 =$ **HK$300** |
| Example limit-style price | ~**HK$1,190** | ~**HK$290** |

When policy or contracts force **sharing** of scarce pads, the incumbent’s “moat” from sunk infrastructure shrinks and limit prices fall. The arithmetic estimates a break-even screen — it does not prove that limit pricing always deters entry.

**Tool chain.** High sunk pad costs raise $AC_{\text{Entrant}}$ → higher possible $P_{\text{Limit}}$ → incumbent can charge more *while* watching entry. Shared-pad policy reverses that. Co-opetition ([§10](#10-co-opetition-compete-on-service-share-the-roof)) is one institutional way to lower sunk entry — if governance works.

## 8. Hong Kong experimentation and GBA scale

Competitive strategy in this course is HK-first but GBA-aware:

- **GBA strengths** often sit in aircraft, electronics, batteries, and supply chains.  
- **Hong Kong** may contribute dense urban testing plus finance, insurance, logistics, legal, and professional services.  
- **Sandbox X** (distinct from the earlier Regulatory Sandbox) supports controlled trials that generate evidence and reduce uncertainty — still **not** a waiver of safety rules and **not** automatic commercial approval.  
- Cross-boundary ideas need coordination on routes, customs, data, communications, and safety.

### Absolute programme facts (do not invent shares)

| Fact | Issuer-backed reading on this site |
|------|-------------------------------------|
| First Regulatory Sandbox batch **38 of 72** | [Key figures](key-figures.qmd) · GIA 20 Mar 2025 |
| Sandbox X selected modules **33** so far (UTM 15 + unconventional 4 + shared platform 5 + others 9) | [Key figures](key-figures.qmd) · TLB |
| “~10” Sandbox X projects that had begun testing | Policy Address snapshot — **not** the same as 33 modules |
| Trial ≠ dominance | [Who decides what? · standing caveats](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats) |

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Corridor caveat.** A Shenzhen–Hong Kong / GBA cross-boundary corridor appears in policy discussion, but on the evidence tracked here it is **not** day-to-day operating corridor service. Sandbox X may include cross-boundary *trials* (AC-017 on later week Readings) — trials are not a scheduled product ([Regulators · standing caveats](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats); [Official status](tracker.qmd)).
:::

Hong Kong’s service-layer role is a **strategy to build**, not an automatic outcome (same theme as Week 1 / OHKF supporting-services framing — still a think-tank projection, not government GDP).

## 9. Price competition when capacity is scarce

### Bertrand intuition

If two operators offer a homogeneous service with **unconstrained** capacity, price undercutting can drive price down toward **marginal cost** — a “race to the bottom” where margins vanish (Bertrand-style teaching model):

$$
P = MC \quad \text{(unconstrained capacity, homogeneous product)}
$$

### Why scarce pads change the story

In land-scarce settings, vertiport or pad rules may cap how many movements each operator can run. If **total capacity is below demand**, neither firm can serve the whole market by cutting price alone. Capacity constraints **may soften** price wars. Reliability, schedule, access quality, and brand can also differentiate services.

Capacity limits do **not** guarantee high prices or profits: allocation rules, regulation, demand shocks, and quality still matter. Week 8 returns to congestion and slot logic.

### Worked illustration (capacity vs price war)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** $MC =$ HK$100; willingness to pay up to HK$500; demand = 100 passengers.

| | Unconstrained fleets | Each limited to 30 flights/day (total 60 < 100) |
|--|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Logic | Undercutting can push $P$ toward **HK$100** | Neither can absorb all demand; price pressure **may** be weaker |
| Lesson | Price war destroys margins | Scarcity can support margins — not a promise of $P =$ HK$500 |

### Beyond the slide: connecting Bertrand to ATC and HHI

- If ATC is HK$1,717 at low utilization ([§5](#worked-illustration-rooftop-rent)), a Bertrand outcome at $P=MC=\text{HK\$50}$ is **financially ruinous** — firms will exit or seek pad scarcity / differentiation.  
- If pads are shared and capacity expands, Bertrand pressure can return — which is why co-opetition needs **access rules**, not only a lower rent bill ([§10](#10-co-opetition-compete-on-service-share-the-roof)).  
- High HHI on a pad-constrained corridor may coexist with soft price competition — or with regulated access prices. HHI alone cannot tell which.

---

## 10. Co-opetition: compete on service, share the roof

Airlines sometimes compete for passengers while sharing lounges or codeshares. Early LAE operators may need a similar split:

- **Compete** on vehicle, app experience, reliability, and brand.  
- **Cooperate** on scarce landing sites, charging, or digital traffic coordination where duplication is ruinously expensive.

**Co-opetition** only lowers unit cost if rules for **access, investment, control, congestion, data, liability, and competition law** are clear. Sharing without governance can recreate conflict. Week 6 deepens PPP / payment design; Week 8 deepens shared facility cost per movement.

Teaching split of a shared fixed infrastructure cost among $N$ operators:

$$
\text{Savings per operator relative to going alone} = \frac{\text{Fixed infrastructure cost} \times (N-1)}{N}
$$

### Worked illustration (shared rooftop)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** Kowloon rooftop site **HK$100,000/day**.

| | Alone | Four operators share equally |
|--|-------|------------------------------|
| Fixed cost per operator | HK$100,000 | HK$25,000 |
| If each flies 100 times/day | HK$1,000 rent/flight | HK$250 rent/flight |

Sharing is one of the fastest ways to survive extreme land costs — if the access rules work.

**Link to limit pricing.** Shared pads cut sunk entry ([§7](#worked-illustration-limit-price-and-shared-pads)) and can raise Bertrand pressure ([§9](#9-price-competition-when-capacity-is-scarce)). Co-opetition is not “free money”: it trades a lower cost floor for harder price competition and governance cost.

## 11. Global comparators (not Hong Kong law)

Firms adapt entry strategy to how each jurisdiction sequences trials, certification, infrastructure, and deployment:

- **Hong Kong** — sandboxes (including **Sandbox X** for more complex trials) generate controlled evidence. Keep **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**.  
- **Europe (U-space framing)** — digital traffic rules and services as a structured comparator. **U-space is not Hong Kong law** ([Glossary · airspace](glossary.qmd#airspace-and-traffic)).  
- **USA (e.g. FAA Innovate28-style planning)** — implementation plans coordinating certification, operations, airspace, infrastructure, environment, and community engagement.

Use these as **comparators** on [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd) and [Readings](#readings) — not as plug-in Hong Kong compliance checklists. Shenzhen’s LAE industry-promotion ordinance and NDRC diffusion notices on this week’s Readings illustrate **institutional** competition settings in the GBA — still not a claim about any operator’s market share.

---

## 12. Putting Week 2 together

Define the market narrowly. Measure concentration only as a **screen** (HHI). Trace average cost to **fixed sites + utilization/density**. Treat NASA-style barriers and **sunk costs** as the material of moats and **limit pricing**. Expect **Bertrand-style** pressure when capacity is loose; expect softer price wars when pads bind — without assuming profits. Use **co-opetition** when shared infrastructure beats duplication, with governance attached.

Keep **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**, and never confuse trial participation (38 of 72 / Sandbox X modules) with proven dominance. Do not claim GBA corridors as day-to-day service.

The short checklist is in [Summary](#summary) above.

---

## 13. Study checklist (beyond the slides)

1. Define a **narrow market** (product + geography + customer + layer) before talking about competition.  
2. Explain why LAE is **not one market structure**.  
3. Compute **HHI** from percent shares and interpret it only as a **screen**.  
4. Separate **fixed** vs **marginal** cost; compute **ATC** at low and high utilization.  
5. Contrast **economies of scale** (bigger vehicles) with **economies of density** (more volume on the same sites).  
6. List NASA-style barriers and give a **sunk cost** example that is hard to resell.  
7. Compute a teaching **limit price** and show how shared pads change it.  
8. State Bertrand $P=MC$ under unconstrained capacity — and why **pad caps** may soften wars.  
9. Explain **co-opetition**: what is shared, what stays competitive, what governance is required.  
10. Keep **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**; cite **38 of 72** and Sandbox X **33** modules without inventing shares.  
11. State the **corridor caveat**: policy / trial ≠ day-to-day operating service.  
12. Connect the chain: scarce pads → density → ATC → entry / limit price → Bertrand or co-opetition.
